questions.stem: Which of these is a non-infectious disease?
options: Malaria
Whooping cough (pertussis)
Cystic fibrosis
Tuberculosis
questions.explanation: Cystic fibrosis is an inherited genetic disorder, so it cannot be passed from person to person by a pathogen. Tuberculosis (a bacterium), malaria (a protist) and tinea (a fungus) are all caused by pathogens and are infectious.

questions.stem: What is a prion?
options: A eukaryotic parasite that lives inside nerve cells
A misfolded protein that causes normal proteins to misfold
A non-cellular particle of RNA inside a protein capsid coat
A prokaryotic cell that has lost its cell wall
questions.explanation: A prion is an infectious protein with an abnormal shape that converts normal copies of the protein into the misfolded form. Prions contain no nucleic acid, which is what distinguishes them from viruses.

questions.stem: Which feature is shared by all viruses?
options: Nucleic acid enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid
A lipid envelope taken from the host cell's membrane
Ribosomes that make viral proteins from viral RNA
A cell wall made of peptidoglycan surrounding the genome
questions.explanation: Every virus has DNA or RNA inside a protein capsid. Only some viruses, such as influenza, also have an envelope. Viruses have no ribosomes, so they must use the host cell's ribosomes to make proteins.

questions.stem: Why are antibiotics ineffective against influenza?
options: Influenza viruses multiply outside cells, where antibiotics are unable to reach
Influenza is caused by a virus, which lacks the bacterial structures antibiotics target
Influenza is caused by a bacterium that is protected from antibiotics by its capsule
Antibiotics are broken down by the high fever that influenza usually causes
questions.explanation: Antibiotics act on structures and processes found in bacteria, such as peptidoglycan cell walls and bacterial ribosomes. Viruses have none of these and replicate inside host cells using the host's machinery.

questions.stem: A unicellular eukaryotic pathogen is passed to humans by a mosquito and then infects liver cells and red blood cells. Which type of pathogen is it?
options: Virus
Fungus
Protist
Bacterium
questions.explanation: This describes Plasmodium, the cause of malaria. It is a single-celled eukaryote, so it is a protist. Bacteria are prokaryotes, and viruses are not cells at all.

questions.stem: A pathogen grows as thread-like hyphae with cell walls of chitin, spreads by spores and causes itchy, cracked skin between the toes. What type of pathogen is it?
options: Protist
Prion
Fungus
Bacterium
questions.explanation: Hyphae, chitin cell walls and spores are features of fungi; this describes tinea (athlete's foot). Bacteria are single prokaryotic cells with peptidoglycan walls and do not form hyphae of this kind.

questions.stem: Tapeworms and head lice are both examples of:
options: fungal pathogens
prokaryotic pathogens
multicellular parasites
unicellular protists
questions.explanation: Tapeworms (living inside the gut) and lice (living on the scalp) are multicellular animals that live on or in a host and harm it, so they are parasites. Protists are mostly single-celled.

questions.stem: How do pili on the surface of some bacteria help them cause disease?
options: They attach the bacteria to host cells so the bacteria are not flushed away
They digest the connective tissue so the bacteria can spread through it
They coat the bacteria so that phagocytes are unable to engulf and digest them
They release toxins that damage the plasma membranes of nearby host cells
questions.explanation: Pili are adherence factors: they bind to receptors on host cells, so the bacteria can colonise surfaces such as the urinary tract without being washed away. Preventing engulfment is the role of a capsule.

questions.stem: Some bacteria secrete enzymes, such as hyaluronidase, that break down the material holding host cells together. These enzymes are best described as:
options: adherence factors that help the bacteria attach to host cells
endotoxins released from the bacterial wall when the cells die
capsules that protect the bacteria from attack by complement
invasion factors that help the bacteria spread through tissues
questions.explanation: Enzymes that break down tissue components let bacteria penetrate and spread through host tissues, so they are invasion factors. Adherence factors such as pili only attach bacteria to cell surfaces.

questions.stem: Strains of Streptococcus pneumoniae with a capsule cause pneumonia, while strains without a capsule are usually cleared by the immune system. What best explains this?
options: The capsule helps the bacteria avoid being engulfed by phagocytes
The capsule produces toxins that destroy cells of the lung lining
The capsule allows the bacteria to enter the nuclei of host cells
The capsule makes the bacteria resistant to all known antibiotics
questions.explanation: A slippery polysaccharide capsule makes it hard for phagocytes such as neutrophils and macrophages to engulf the bacteria, so they survive and multiply. The capsule is not a toxin and does not provide antibiotic resistance.

questions.stem: Clostridium tetani secretes a protein that blocks the release of inhibitory neurotransmitters, causing severe muscle spasms. How is this protein classified?
options: An invasion factor
An exotoxin
An endotoxin
An adherence factor
questions.explanation: Exotoxins are proteins secreted by living bacteria, and tetanus toxin is a classic example. Endotoxins are lipopolysaccharides that form part of the outer membrane of some bacteria and are released mainly when the cells die.

questions.stem: How do a person's immune cells recognise the person's own body cells as self?
options: By reading the DNA sequence inside each cell's nucleus
By the person's own MHC markers displayed on the cell surface
By the antibodies that each body cell produces and secretes itself
By the complete absence of proteins on the cell surface
questions.explanation: Body cells display MHC markers that are specific to the individual, and immune cells learn to tolerate these as self. Cells or particles with different markers or foreign antigens are recognised as non-self.

questions.stem: Which is part of the first line of defence in vertebrates?
options: Neutrophils engulfing bacteria
Complement proteins in the plasma
Antibodies produced by plasma cells
Mucus and cilia lining the airways
questions.explanation: The first line of defence is made up of barriers such as skin and mucous membranes, which stop pathogens entering. Neutrophils and complement are part of the second line, and antibodies are part of the third.

questions.stem: Which correctly matches each response to its line of defence?
options: Inflammation: second line; antibody production: third line
Inflammation: first line; antibody production: second line
Inflammation: third line; antibody production: second line
Inflammation: second line; antibody production: first line
questions.explanation: The inflammatory response and complement system form the non-specific second line of defence. Antibody production by plasma cells is part of the specific adaptive response, the third line.

questions.stem: During inflammation, what is the role of prostaglandins?
options: They promote vasodilation and increase sensitivity to pain
They bind to bacterial toxins and neutralise them in the blood
They kill virus-infected cells by triggering their apoptosis
They form pores that cause bacterial cells to burst open
questions.explanation: Prostaglandins are signalling molecules released at a damaged site. They cause blood vessels to dilate, which brings more blood, and they sensitise nerve endings, which is why inflamed areas are painful. Neutralising toxins is the role of antibodies.

questions.stem: Which white blood cells are usually the first to arrive at a site of infection, where they engulf bacteria?
options: Memory B cells
Neutrophils
Plasma cells
Cytotoxic T cells
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the most abundant white blood cells and move quickly into infected tissue, where they phagocytose bacteria. Plasma cells and T cells belong to the adaptive response, which takes days to develop.

questions.stem: As well as engulfing pathogens, macrophages link the innate and adaptive responses. How?
options: They kill infected body cells by releasing perforin and granzymes
They divide to form memory cells that persist for many years
They present antigen fragments on MHC markers to helper T cells
They secrete antibodies that match the antigens of the pathogen
questions.explanation: After digesting a pathogen, a macrophage displays fragments of its antigens on MHC class II markers. Helper T cells with matching receptors are activated, starting the adaptive response. Antibodies are secreted by plasma cells, not macrophages.

questions.stem: Which cells do natural killer (NK) cells destroy?
options: Virus-infected and cancerous body cells, without needing earlier exposure
Bacteria in the blood, by releasing antibodies that cause the cells to clump
Only cells displaying an antigen that they met in an earlier infection
Pathogens in the gut, by secreting digestive enzymes into the gut lumen
questions.explanation: NK cells are part of the innate response and kill abnormal body cells, such as those infected by viruses or cancerous cells, by triggering apoptosis. Because they are innate, they do not need prior exposure and do not form memory.

questions.stem: Which is a role of the complement system?
options: Recognising infected cells by the viral antigen on their MHC markers
Producing memory cells that give long-term protection after infection
Forming pores in bacterial membranes that cause the cells to burst
Producing antibodies that are specific to a single type of antigen
questions.explanation: Complement is a group of plasma proteins that can form membrane attack complexes, which punch holes in bacterial membranes. Complement also coats pathogens to aid phagocytosis and attracts phagocytes, but it is non-specific and forms no memory.

questions.stem: In the humoral response, a B cell that binds a specific antigen is activated and divides. What cells does it produce?
options: Helper T cells that release cytokines, and natural killer cells
Plasma cells that secrete antibodies, and memory B cells
Cytotoxic T cells that kill infected cells, and memory T cells
Macrophages that engulf the antigen, and more neutrophils
questions.explanation: An activated B cell undergoes clonal expansion to form plasma cells, which secrete antibodies matching the antigen, and memory B cells, which allow a faster response later. T cells come from a separate lineage.

questions.stem: A virus has entered body cells and is replicating inside them. Which response can eliminate these infected cells?
options: Antibodies entering the infected cells and binding to the virus
Plasma cells engulfing the infected cells by phagocytosis
Memory B cells releasing perforin onto the infected cells
Cytotoxic T cells destroying the cells that display viral antigen
questions.explanation: Antibodies act on antigens outside cells and cannot reach a virus replicating inside a cell. The cell-mediated response deals with infected cells: cytotoxic T cells recognise viral antigen displayed on MHC class I markers and kill the cell.

questions.stem: A person's antibody level is measured after a first and a second exposure to the same antigen, two months apart. How does the second response compare with the first?
options: It starts later but reaches a higher level, because of plasma cells left from the first
It is the same size and speed, because antibodies are made from scratch each time
It is smaller, because old antibodies are still neutralising most of the antigen
It starts sooner, reaches a higher level and lasts longer, because of memory cells
questions.explanation: Memory B cells formed in the first response recognise the antigen quickly and rapidly produce many plasma cells. The secondary response therefore has a shorter lag, a much higher peak and a longer duration. Plasma cells are short-lived, so they do not explain it.

questions.stem: A graph of an infant's blood antibodies shows maternal antibodies falling to near zero by about six months, while the infant's own antibodies rise after vaccinations. Why do the maternal antibodies fall?
options: They give passive immunity: no memory cells form, so they are broken down and not replaced
They give active immunity: memory cells form, so the antibodies are no longer needed
The infant's vaccinations destroy the maternal antibodies as soon as they are given
The infant's kidneys excrete the maternal antibodies because they are recognised as self
questions.explanation: Antibodies received from the mother are passive immunity. The infant has no memory cells or plasma cells making these antibodies, so they are gradually broken down. The infant's own active immunity, from vaccination, produces lasting memory cells.

questions.stem: Antibodies in breast milk protect a breastfed baby's gut from infection. What type of immunity is this?
options: Artificially acquired passive immunity
Artificially acquired active immunity
Naturally acquired passive immunity
Naturally acquired active immunity
questions.explanation: The antibodies are made by the mother, not the baby, so the immunity is passive. They are received through a normal process rather than a medical procedure, so it is naturally acquired.

questions.stem: An unvaccinated patient with a deep, dirty wound is given an injection of tetanus immunoglobulin (antibodies). What type of immunity does this give?
options: Naturally acquired active immunity
Artificially acquired passive immunity
Artificially acquired active immunity
Naturally acquired passive immunity
questions.explanation: Ready-made antibodies injected by a health worker give artificially acquired passive immunity. The patient's own lymphocytes are not stimulated to make antibodies or memory cells, so protection is immediate but short-lived. A vaccine would give active immunity.

questions.stem: Compared with active immunity, passive immunity is:
options: immediate and lifelong, because the antibodies are self-renewing
slow to develop and short-lived, because few antibodies are made
immediate but short-lived, because no memory cells are formed
slow to develop but lifelong, because memory cells are formed
questions.explanation: Passive immunity provides ready-made antibodies, so protection begins at once, but the antibodies are broken down within weeks to months and no memory cells form. Active immunity takes time to develop but leaves memory cells.

questions.stem: Which is a physical defence of plants against pathogens?
options: A thick waxy cuticle on the leaf surface
Defensins that disrupt fungal membranes
Toxic alkaloids such as nicotine
Antibodies produced in the phloem sap
questions.explanation: The cuticle is a physical barrier that pathogens must break through to reach leaf cells. Defensins and alkaloid toxins are chemical defences. Plants do not produce antibodies.

questions.stem: Plant defensins are best described as:
options: hairs on the leaf surface that trap insects carrying pathogens
small antimicrobial proteins that disrupt pathogen membranes
thick layers of cellulose that block the growth of fungal hyphae
white blood cells carried in the xylem to sites of infection
questions.explanation: Defensins are small proteins produced by plants that act against pathogens, especially fungi, often by disrupting their membranes. They are a chemical defence, whereas thickened cell walls and leaf hairs are physical defences.

questions.stem: Paper discs (6 mm wide) soaked in three antimicrobial agents were placed on agar spread with bacteria. Mean diameters of the clear zones: X 22 mm, Y 9 mm, Z 6 mm. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Y was most effective, as its zone was closest in size to the disc
X inhibited the bacteria most, and Z showed no detectable effect
Z was most effective, as it allowed the least growth near its disc
All three were effective, as each one produced a zone of 6 mm or more
questions.explanation: A larger clear zone means the agent inhibited bacterial growth over a greater distance. A zone of 6 mm is just the disc itself, so Z had no measurable effect. Zone size also depends on how well each agent diffuses, so it compares agents only under the same conditions.

questions.stem: Which pairing of a disease and its main mode of transmission is correct?
options: Cholera: contaminated water
Malaria: contaminated food
Hepatitis B: mosquito vector
Tinea: mosquito vector
questions.explanation: Cholera bacteria spread in water contaminated with faeces. Malaria is spread by mosquitoes, hepatitis B by contact with infected blood and other body fluids, and tinea by direct contact with infected skin or surfaces.

questions.stem: Dengue fever is spread to people by Aedes mosquitoes. In this disease, the mosquito is the:
options: reservoir, in which the virus is always destroyed
primary host, in which the symptoms first appear
vector, carrying the virus between human hosts
pathogen, causing the symptoms of the disease
questions.explanation: A vector is an organism that carries a pathogen from one host to another. The dengue virus is the pathogen; the mosquito transmits it when it feeds on blood.

questions.stem: Pathogen P makes people bedridden within a day of infection. Pathogen Q causes mild symptoms, and infected people stay infectious for weeks while going about daily life. Both spread by droplets. Which is likely to spread more widely?
options: Q, because mild symptoms mean the pathogen mutates much more slowly
Q, because infected people remain infectious for longer while moving freely
P, because a short time before symptoms means more people are infected
P, because severe symptoms release a larger total number of pathogens
questions.explanation: The longer a pathogen persists in a host that is still mobile, the more people that host can infect. People severely ill with P stay at home, which limits their contacts. Persistence and mobility, not symptom severity, drive spread here.

questions.stem: Why does vaccinating a high proportion of a population also protect people who cannot be vaccinated?
options: The vaccine spreads from vaccinated people to unvaccinated people by contact
Vaccinated people kill the pathogen in the environment before it reaches others
The pathogen has few susceptible hosts to pass to, so chains of transmission break
Vaccinated people release antibodies into the air that protect those around them
questions.explanation: When most people are immune, an infected person is unlikely to meet a susceptible person, so transmission chains end before reaching those who are unprotected. This is herd immunity. Antibodies are not passed between people through the air.

questions.stem: Why can a new respiratory disease spread between continents far faster today than it could a century ago?
options: Modern buildings let pathogens survive longer than old ones did
Air travel moves infected people across the world within a day
Pathogens today reproduce faster than they did a century ago
People today have weaker immune systems than they did then
questions.explanation: The mobility of individuals affects how far and fast a disease spreads. International air travel can carry an infected person, who may not yet show symptoms, to another continent before the disease is detected.

questions.stem: What is quarantine?
options: Restricting the movement of people who may have been exposed but are not yet ill
Treating people who are already ill in a separate, closed ward of a hospital
Identifying and listing everyone who has had contact with an ill person
Vaccinating everyone living in a region where cases have been reported
questions.explanation: Quarantine separates people who may have been exposed until it is clear whether they are infected. Separating people who are already ill is isolation, and identifying contacts is contact tracing.

questions.stem: How does contact tracing help to control an outbreak?
options: Vectors are traced back to their breeding sites so that they can be destroyed
Everyone in the region is tested to find the people with the most symptoms
Exposed people are found early so they can be tested, treated or quarantined
Infected people are given antibodies so they can no longer spread the pathogen
questions.explanation: Contact tracing identifies people who have been near a confirmed case so they can be tested, treated or quarantined before they pass the pathogen on. Combined with personal hygiene measures such as handwashing, it breaks chains of transmission.

questions.stem: After a wedding, 64 of 120 guests fell ill. Chicken: 60 of 80 who ate it fell ill, and 4 of 40 who did not. Salad: 32 of 60 who ate it, and 32 of 60 who did not. Prawns: 30 of 50 who ate them, and 34 of 70 who did not. Which food was most likely the source?
options: Prawns, because 60% of the guests who ate them fell ill, which is above half
Chicken, because more guests ate the chicken than ate any of the other foods
Chicken, because 75% of those who ate it fell ill compared with 10% of those who did not
Salad, because the same number of guests who ate it and did not eat it fell ill
questions.explanation: The likely source is the food with the biggest difference in illness rate between those who ate it and those who did not: 75% versus 10% for chicken. For salad the rates are equal (53%), and for prawns they are similar (60% versus 49%).

questions.stem: An epidemic curve for a gastrointestinal illness shows cases rising sharply to a single peak within two days and then falling to zero. What does this pattern suggest?
options: An airborne disease brought in by travellers arriving over several weeks
A point source, such as one contaminated meal, exposed people at the same time
Person-to-person spread through several successive generations of cases
A vector-borne disease that spread as mosquito numbers rose over a season
questions.explanation: A single sharp peak means most people were infected at about the same time from a common source. Person-to-person spread produces a series of rising waves spaced about one incubation period apart.

questions.stem: In region A, measles cases fell from about 400 a year to 20 a year after vaccination coverage rose from 70% to 95%. In nearby region B, where coverage stayed at 70%, cases stayed near 380 a year. What does the comparison suggest?
options: The rise in coverage, not a change affecting both regions, most likely caused the fall
Measles became less infectious in both regions, so vaccination had little effect
Region B must have had a more dangerous strain of measles than region A had
Vaccination coverage above 70% has no further effect on the spread of measles
questions.explanation: Region B acts as a comparison: if something affecting both regions, such as a milder strain, had caused the fall, cases would have fallen in B too. Only A, where coverage rose, saw the decline, which supports the vaccination program's effectiveness.

questions.stem: In 1854, John Snow mapped cholera deaths in a London district and found that they clustered around one public water pump. What did this analysis mainly help to determine?
options: The incubation period of the disease and its symptoms
The proportion of the local population that was immune
The source of the outbreak and its mode of transmission
The structure of the pathogen and how it reproduces
questions.explanation: Mapping cases showed a cluster around the Broad Street pump, pointing to contaminated water as the source and the route of transmission. The cholera bacterium itself was not identified by this method.
